courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Instantaneous power in an AC circuit: p(t) = v(t)i(t) at every instant, so the DC relation P = VI survives only as an instantaneous statement and must be averaged over a whole cycle before it can be called the power

Decomposition of the instantaneous power: with v = V0 sin(wt) and i = I0 sin(wt - phi), p(t) = (V0*I0/2)[cos(phi) - cos(2wt - phi)], a constant term plus a ripple at twice the supply frequency whose average over a cycle is zero

The master formula P_av = (1/2)V0*I0*cos(phi) = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = Irms^2 * R, so that only the resistance dissipates and a pure reactance consumes no average power however large its current and voltage

Real, reactive and apparent power distinguished: P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) in watts, Q = Vrms*Irms*sin(phi) in volt-amperes reactive, S = Vrms*Irms in volt-amperes, forming a right-angled power triangle with S^2 = P^2 + Q^2 and tan(phi) = Q/P

Power factor PF = P/S = cos(phi) = R/Z, dimensionless and between 0 and 1, with the sign of phi carried separately as lagging (inductive, Q positive) or leading (capacitive, Q negative) since cos(phi) is an even function

The sign of the instantaneous power: p(t) oscillates about P with amplitude S, so its minimum S(cos(phi) - 1) is negative in any circuit with a net reactance and zero only when phi = 0; negative p means energy returning to the source, and for a pure L or C the positive and negative areas cancel exactly

Element by element: a resistor has p = P(1 - cos 2wt) swinging from 0 to 2P and never negative; an inductor has p = -Vrms*Irms*sin(2wt) with zero mean, storing up to (1/2)L*I0^2 in the magnetic field and returning it; a capacitor behaves identically with the electric field and the opposite sign of Q

Practical consequences: power-factor correction by a parallel capacitor with Q_C = P[tan(phi1) - tan(phi2)] and C = Q_C/(w*Vrms^2), which leaves P unchanged while cutting the line current and the I^2 R feeder loss; and series resonance at X_L = X_C, w0 = 1/sqrt(LC), where Z falls to R, PF = 1 and the real power Vrms^2/R is a maximum

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: The indefinite integral of f is the whole family of its antiderivatives: (integral of f(x) dx) = F(x) + C means F'(x) = f(x), and the arbitrary constant is there because any two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant

The power rule for integration, (integral of x^n dx) = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for every n except n = -1 - raise the power, then divide by the new power, after rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers - with the excluded case filled by (integral of dx/x) = ln|x| + C, whose modulus is needed because 1/x is defined for negative x while ln x is not

Integration is linear - it splits over sums and differences and lets constant multiples out - but there is no product, quotient or chain rule for integration, so products must be expanded, quotients divided out and composites substituted before anything can be integrated

Standard forms: sin x -> -cos x, cos x -> sin x, sec^2 x -> tan x, e^x -> e^x, e^(kx) -> e^(kx)/k, a^x -> a^x/ln a, and 1/(ax + b) -> (1/a) ln|ax + b|, where integration divides by the inner derivative exactly where differentiation multiplied by it, and only when that inner function is linear

Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule: setting u = g(x) with du = g'(x) dx turns the integral into one in u alone, which works only when the inner derivative is already present up to a constant multiple, and in a definite integral the limits must be converted to u-values or the answer converted back to x

The definite integral (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) is a number - the limit of the Riemann sums, sum of f(x_i*) times delta x - read either as the net signed area between the curve and the x-axis over [a, b] or as the total accumulated change of a quantity whose rate of change is f

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, d/dx of (integral from a to x of f(t) dt) = f(x) and (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F, together with the properties (zero width, reversal of limits, additivity over intervals, average value) and the split-at-the-roots method for total area as opposed to signed area

Applications: recovering a curve from its gradient function by fixing C from a given point, and recovering velocity and displacement from acceleration and velocity, where displacement is the integral of v and distance travelled needs the total-area treatment

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: A programme is a series of instructions that causes a computer or a microcontroller to perform a particular task; it also contains data and the memory addresses in which the instructions work, and is written in a programming language such as C, C++, Rust, Assembly, Java or Python

A data type is used for specifying the type of a variable; data types determine the type and size of the data associated with variables, and the three basic types in C are characters (char, 1 byte), integers (int, typically 4 bytes, exact within its range) and floating-point numbers (float 4 bytes, double 8 bytes, approximate to a fixed number of significant digits)

Variable definition always includes 'data type' followed by 'variable name'; a variable definition is also a declaration but not all declarations are definitions - a declaration gives the compiler a name and a type, a definition additionally reserves the storage, and 'extern int total;' declares without defining

The rules governing a variable name in C: letters, digits and the underscore only, never beginning with a digit, no spaces or other punctuation, never a keyword, and case-sensitive; and variable names are not stored inside the computer memory - the compiler replaces them with memory location addresses, so the name exists only at compile time

The six operator categories the course lists - arithmetic (+ - * / % ++ --), relational (== != > < >= <=), logical (&& || !), bitwise (& | ^ ~ << >>), assignment (= += -= etc) and misc (sizeof, address-of &, dereference *, ?: and the cast) - with relational and logical operators yielding the int 1 or 0 and assignment yielding the value it stored

Precedence and associativity: unary -> * / % -> + - -> << >> -> < <= > >= -> == != -> & -> ^ -> | -> && -> || -> ?: -> assignment -> comma, with the binary operators associating left to right and the unary operators, ?: and assignment associating right to left; short-circuit evaluation means && skips its right operand when the left is false and || skips it when the left is true

The operand types choose the operation, not the variable being assigned to: 7 / 2 is the int 3 because both operands are int and the fractional part is truncated towards zero, so a cast must be applied to an operand ((float) a / b) and never to the result ((float)(a / b)); and '5' is the char code 53, 5 is the int, and "5" is a two-character string

Programme objects: real-world objects have two main characteristics, state and behaviour, and in a programme the state of an object is stored in variables while the behaviour is described by methods; only the methods of a particular object have access to that object's variables, and different objects interact only through their own methods, which is information hiding and is controlled by the access specifiers public and private

Structures, unions and classes: a structure is a user-defined data type grouping items of possibly different types into a single type, defined with struct and accessed with the dot syntax, each member having its own storage; a union is defined the same way but all its members start at the same location in memory so it can represent the value of only one member at a time; a class is like a structure but also has methods or functions

Why use programme objects: objects are not dependent on each other so each can be independently created and maintained, an object can be used in various parts of the programme, a faulty object can be removed and replaced without disturbing the rest of the code (similar to how a car works), and because state is reachable only through methods we control how much we share with the outside world - giving modularity, code reusability and independence

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Aim of the experiment: study the discharge of a capacitor, determine the time constant tau, determine the experimental capacitance C, and calculate the percentage error for C

Theory of the capacitor: two conductors separated by a distance d with plate area A and a dielectric of permittivity epsilon, so C = epsilon*A/d; the stored charge is Q = CV; capacitors pass AC and block DC and are used as filters in DC supplies, energy-storage banks for pulsed lasers, timing control, backup power and voltage stabilisation

Discharge law: once the switch key is opened the capacitor voltage decays exponentially as V(t) = V0 * e^(-t/tau), the mirror of last week's charging law V(t) = V0 * (1 - e^(-t/tau)); at t = 0 the voltmeter reads maximum and the curve falls asymptotically to zero

Time constant: tau = RC in seconds with R in ohms and C in farads, and putting t = tau in the discharge equation gives V = V0 * e^(-1) = 0.3679*V0, so tau is the time for the voltage to fall to 36.8 percent of its maximum (against 63.2 percent gained when charging), with the capacitor effectively empty after about 5 tau

Apparatus and circuit: voltmeter, power supply, discharging circuit (capacitor, resistor, switch key), stopwatch and wires in the Praxilabs virtual RC Circuit Discharging laboratory, with the voltmeter connected in parallel across the capacitor

Procedure in order: connect the circuit, set the supply output voltage, close the switch key until the voltmeter reaches its maximum, then open the switch key and start the stopwatch at that instant, recording the voltmeter reading every 10 seconds for at least 7 (preferably 10) readings before ending the trial and downloading the data sheet

Data analysis and the two graphs: plot V on the y-axis against t on the x-axis and read tau where V = 0.3679*V0; then linearise as ln V(t) = ln V0 - t/tau and plot ln V against t to get a straight line of gradient -1/tau and intercept ln V0, the two values of tau having to agree

Calculations and errors: obtain C = tau/R and percentage error = (theoretical - experimental)/theoretical x 100, worked for the sample trial (V0 = 11 V, R = 15 kohm, nominal C = 2200 microfarads, theoretical tau = 33.0 s, graph tau about 32.9 s giving C about 2193 microfarads and 0.3 percent error), plus precautions and sources of error such as reaction time, voltmeter loading and dielectric leakage (both of which shorten the measured tau), lead resistance and component tolerance

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings regardless of race, sex, nationality, ethnicity, language, religion or any other status, and Article 1 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights holds that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, endowed with reason and conscience and bound to act towards one another in the spirit of brotherhood; they include the right to life and liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, freedom of opinion and expression, and the right to work and education

In Nigeria human rights are contained in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, Sections 33 to 46, and the African Charter on Human and People's Rights also guarantees that they are enforceable in Nigerian courts of law, the rights named for Nigeria being freedom of religion, freedom of speech, the right to education, freedom of movement and the right to life

A human rights abuse is anything that harms someone's human rights, including harm to people, communities and the environment; the 1979 Constitution introduced Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy alongside Fundamental Human Rights, shortcomings and inhibitions remain in the 2009 Rules, and the National Human Rights Commission received 1,701,519 cases of rights violations in 2021 against 1,287,280 complaints in 2020, the five common abuses named being extra-judicial killing, rape, restriction of freedom of expression, child marriage and domestic violence

Extra-judicial killing: the Nigerian security forces, particularly the police and military, have been implicated in extrajudicial killings, torture and excessive use of force, the #EndSARS protests of October 2020 brought international attention to police brutality, and the categories given are law enforcement officials, non-state actors, death sentences and deaths in custody due to the use of force or failure to protect the right to life

Rape is a serious human rights abuse in Nigeria, with about 367,000 women and gender-related issues recorded in 2021, obstructed by social stigma, underreporting of cases, inadequate legal frameworks, lack of access to justice and limited support services for survivors; and freedom of expression is restricted, with journalists threatened, intimidated, arrested and detained over political corruption and security, and much of the electronic media controlled through the National Broadcasting Commission's regulatory oversight of television and radio stations

Child marriage is prohibited under international law, and a State violates that law if it fails to establish a minimum age of marriage, enforce it, provide for and enforce the same minimum age for boys and girls, act with due diligence to prevent it, or if it involves public officials in it; 43% of girls in Nigeria are married before their 18th birthday and 16% before the age of 15 (Aliogo, 2023)

Domestic violence is addressed by the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act signed into law in 2015, which criminalises various forms of abuse and provides mechanisms for reporting, prosecution and support for survivors, though underreporting from social stigma, inadequate enforcement, limited awareness and inaccessible support services persist

The week's framing of democracy and the rule of law: democracy as government of the people, by the people and for the people, built on strong institutions rather than individuals or groups; the rule of law as governance by law rather than arbitrary decisions of officials, resting on supremacy of law, equality before the law and protection of individual rights through the courts; and Nigeria classified as a hybrid state on the Democracy Index, its democracy a work in progress, with the conclusion that human rights are not validated by the number of treaties a government has signed but by domestic enforcement, every agency being bound to enforce the norms of the Constitution and penalties being imposed regardless of socioeconomic class

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Reading strategies defined as techniques and approaches used to enhance reading comprehension, retention and overall effectiveness with written text, helping the reader process information, extract meaning and gain deeper understanding, with SQ3R as one such strategy rather than the whole category
SQ3R read as S + Q + 3R and expanding to five stages in a fixed order: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review

Survey: quickly scanning the entire text before detailed reading, taking in headings, subheadings, images, captions and other structural features, to obtain a sense of the text's structure and main ideas

Question: generating your own questions from what the survey revealed rather than answering the questions supplied by the passage, so that the questions guide the reading and focus it on the most critical information
Read: the first full contact with the prose, with two stated goals - reading to answer the questions you generated, and reading to engage with the material for a fuller understanding

Recite: vocalising your thoughts by reciting or verbally explaining the key points, words and concepts in your own words, described in the summary slide as verbally or mentally summarising what you have learned to reinforce understanding

Review: creating summaries, outlines or notes and revisiting them and the text, the stage tied specifically to maintaining a deep understanding over time and being able to recall and apply it in exams or discussions

The supporting comprehension strategies from the week's summary sheet: context clues as in-text hints to the meaning of unfamiliar words, inference as a logical conclusion drawn from explicit details plus background knowledge, the fact/opinion distinction between the objective and verifiable and the subjective, and explicit meaning (directly stated, no inference) versus implicit meaning (suggested, requiring inference)

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: The Document Object Model is a programming interface that represents an HTML, XHTML or XML document as a tree of objects, so scripts can read and change a page after it has loaded
DOM nodes come in three kinds that the exam distinguishes: element nodes (the tags such as div, button and a), attribute nodes (src, alt, id, class) and text nodes (the text inside an element)
The DOM tree is hierarchical: an element node has a parent node, child nodes and sibling nodes, and the text inside a paragraph is a text-node child of that paragraph rather than of its container
The document object is the entry point to the DOM and represents the whole page; document.title and every selection call start from it

Five selection methods and what each returns: getElementById -> one element or null, getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName -> a live HTMLCollection, querySelector -> the first CSS-selector match or null, querySelectorAll -> a static NodeList of all matches
Content modification with textContent (plain text, markup shown literally) versus innerHTML (parsed HTML), and the cross-site-scripting risk of assigning untrusted input through innerHTML

Attribute modification with getAttribute, setAttribute, removeAttribute and hasAttribute, plus custom data- attributes read through element.dataset, where data-user-id becomes dataset.userId and the value is always a string

Building and removing nodes with createElement (which produces a detached node), appendChild to attach it to the tree and parent.removeChild to take it out, and event handling with addEventListener("click", handler) where the handler is passed rather than called

checks.topic: Conceptual session on Week 7 integration exactly as the lecturer builds it: the definition ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c with F′(x) = f(x); why the constant is forced, via her Example 1 line [G(x) + c]′ = 2x + 0 = 2x; the power rule ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c and the reason n ≠ −1; what splitting an integral does and does not license; and the Fundamental Theorem ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) = F(x)|ₐᵇ, why c cancels there, and why the result is a number.

questions.q: The deck defines the indefinite integral of f as a function F such that a certain equation holds, plus the constant of integration c. Which equation?
questions.concept: Definition of the indefinite integral (slide 4)
questions.why: F is an antiderivative: differentiating F must return the integrand f, so F′(x) = f(x). Option 1 reverses the roles and describes f as the antiderivative of F. Option 2 confuses integration with adding a constant to the integrand — a vertical shift of f, which is not F at all. Option 4 is the Fundamental Theorem's evaluation formula for a definite integral, a number, not the defining property of F.

questions.q: In Example 1 the lecturer says it is 'tempting to suppose' the antiderivative of g(x) = 2x is G(x) = x², then says the situation is not so simple. What exactly is her objection?
options: G is one antiderivative but not the only one, since G(x) + c differentiates to 2x for every real c
G(x) = x² is not actually an antiderivative of 2x; the correct one is x²/2
The antiderivative exists only where 2x is positive
2x cannot be integrated by the power rule because its coefficient is not 1
questions.concept: Why the constant of integration is forced, not decorative
questions.why: Her line [G(x) + c]′ = 2x + 0 = 2x = g(x) shows every member of the family x² + c works, so no single function can be 'the' answer. Option 2 is a differentiation slip — d/dx(x²) = 2x, so x² is correct as far as it goes. Option 3 invents a domain restriction the slide never makes. Option 4 is false; constants are pulled straight out, as Example 4 does.

questions.q: The power rule ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c is stated with the restriction n ≠ −1. What breaks at n = −1?
options: The numerator x^(n+1) becomes x⁰ = 1, so the answer would be a constant, which is uninformative
x⁻¹ takes negative values, and the formula is only valid for non-negative integrands
1/x has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, so it has no antiderivative on any interval
The denominator n + 1 becomes 0, so the formula divides by zero
questions.concept: Why n = −1 is excluded from the power rule
questions.why: n + 1 = 0 makes x^(n+1)/(n+1) an expression with zero in the denominator — undefined, so the rule simply says nothing there. Option 1 notices the numerator correctly but names the wrong failure; a constant numerator would be fine if the denominator were not 0. Option 2 is false — the rule handles n = −7 in Example 3. Option 3 confuses a problem at a single point with a problem on the whole line; 1/x does have antiderivatives on intervals avoiding 0, just not ones this formula produces.

questions.q: Example 3 integrates 2/x⁷, which is positive for every x > 0, yet the answer −1/(3x⁶) + c is negative there. Which step of the lecturer's working introduces the minus sign?
options: Rewriting 2/x⁷ as 2x⁻⁷, because the exponent becomes negative
Dividing by the new power, which is −7 + 1 = −6
Adding the constant of integration c
questions.concept: Where the sign comes from when integrating a negative power
questions.why: The rule divides by the new exponent, and 2 ÷ (−6) = −1/3. Option 1 confuses notation with arithmetic: rewriting a fraction as a negative power changes nothing about the value, and 2x⁻⁷ is still positive for x > 0. Option 3 is wrong because c is an unknown constant, not a sign. Option 4 describes only the reduction of the magnitude, which carries no sign of its own. This distinction is what separates students who apply the rule from those who have memorised the answer.

questions.q: What kind of object does each of ∫f(x)dx and ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx produce?
options: The first a family of functions, the second a number
Both are numbers, but the second one is signed
The first a number, the second a function of a and b
Both are functions of x; the limits only restrict the domain
questions.concept: Indefinite versus definite integral as different kinds of answer
questions.why: The indefinite integral is F(x) + c — the collection of all antiderivatives, hence a family of functions. Slide 11 says of the definite integral that 'the result will usually be a number'. Option 2 misses that an indefinite answer still contains x and an unknown c. Option 3 swaps the two. Option 4 misreads the limits as a domain restriction rather than as inputs to F(b) − F(a); after the substitution no x survives at all.

questions.q: The theorem says ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is an antiderivative of f. Why does it not matter which antiderivative you choose?
options: Because the theorem quietly assumes the antiderivative with c = 0
Because F is unique once f is continuous on [a, b]
Because a and b are constants, so any extra constant is absorbed into them
Any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, and that constant cancels in the subtraction
questions.concept: Why a definite integral carries no constant of integration
questions.why: Using F(x) + c gives (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a); the c disappears by subtraction, which is exactly why definite answers never show + c. Option 1 states a convention where the real reason is an identity — the result holds for every c, not only c = 0. Option 2 contradicts Example 1: antiderivatives are never unique. Option 3 is meaningless; c attaches to F, not to the limits.

questions.q: The lecturer writes ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx = F(x)|ₐᵇ. What does the bar notation instruct you to do?
options: Evaluate f at b and at a and subtract
Evaluate F at b, evaluate F at a, and subtract the second from the first
Restrict F to the interval [a, b]
Evaluate F at a and at b and add the results
questions.concept: Reading the evaluation-bar notation
questions.why: F(x)|ₐᵇ is shorthand for F(b) − F(a), upper limit first. Option 1 substitutes into the integrand instead of the antiderivative — the single most common wrong answer, and the one that turns 18 into 12 in Example 1. Option 3 treats the bar as a domain restriction. Option 4 adds where the theorem subtracts, which would destroy the cancellation of c and give the wrong sign structure entirely.

questions.q: Example 4 rewrites ∫(11x¹⁰ − 4x⁹ + 1)dx as ∫11x¹⁰dx − ∫4x⁹dx + ∫1dx. Which of these moves is NOT justified by anything the deck does?
questions.concept: Splitting is licensed for sums, differences and constant multiples only
questions.why: Products do not split: ∫x⁵dx = x⁶/6, whereas (x³/3)(x⁴/4) = x⁷/12 — different functions, so the move is simply false. Options 1 and 4 are the term-by-term splitting the slide performs. Option 2 is the constant pulled out front, which the slide also does with 11 and 4. A student who has only memorised 'split the integral' will pick one of the legitimate ones.

questions.q: State the deck's definition of the indefinite integral in your own words, and say precisely what role c plays in it.
questions.concept: The definition on slide 4
questions.why: A good answer says: for a continuous real-valued f of x, the indefinite integral is a function F whose derivative is the integrand, F′(x) = f(x), together with an added constant of integration c, written ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c. On c: it is an arbitrary real number, not a placeholder or a unit — it is there because the derivative of any constant is 0, so every function of the form F(x) + c is an equally valid antiderivative, and the notation therefore names the whole family at once.

questions.q: Using the lecturer's own line [G(x) + c]′ = 2x + 0 = 2x = g(x), explain why writing ∫2x dx = x² is an incomplete answer rather than merely an untidy one.
questions.concept: Example 1's argument for the constant of integration
questions.why: A good answer runs the line as an argument: differentiating x² + c gives 2x + 0 = 2x for every real c, so x² + 1, x² − 4 and x² all differentiate to the integrand. Since the question asks for the antiderivatives of 2x, and there are infinitely many, naming only x² names one member of an infinite family and omits the rest. It is incomplete in the way that answering 'x = 2' to x² = 4 is incomplete, not in the way that untidy handwriting is.

questions.q: Explain why a definite integral never carries + c, and show the cancellation explicitly.
questions.concept: Why c disappears under F(b) − F(a)
questions.why: A good answer performs the algebra rather than asserting the rule: take any antiderivative in the form F(x) + c; the theorem gives (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a) + c − c = F(b) − F(a). It should then draw the consequence — every choice of c gives the same number, which is why the theorem can say 'if F(x) is an antiderivative' rather than 'the antiderivative', and why writing + c after a numerical answer is meaningless.

questions.q: The deck never gives an answer to either of its two TASK slides. Describe the method you would use to check your own answer to an indefinite integral, and explain why that check is guaranteed to work.
questions.concept: Verification by differentiation, and why the definition licenses it
questions.why: A good answer names the method — differentiate your result and see whether you recover the integrand — and then justifies it from the definition rather than from habit: ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + c is defined by the condition F′(x) = f(x), so the check is testing exactly the defining condition. It may add that the added c never disturbs the check, since its derivative is 0, and that the check catches the standard errors — multiplying instead of dividing by the new power, or losing a sign on a negative exponent — in a few seconds.

checks.topic: Power in an A.C. circuit as concepts: the instantaneous power p(t) = v(t)i(t) and its oscillation at twice the supply frequency, the derivation of P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi), why a pure reactance dissipates no average power, and the distinction between real, reactive and apparent power with the power factor cos(phi) = R/Z = P/S

questions.q: For v = V0 sin(wt) and i = I0 sin(wt - phi), the instantaneous power p(t) = v*i can be written as a constant plus a single oscillating term. That form is:
questions.concept: Instantaneous power decomposed by the product-to-sum identity
questions.why: sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A-B) - cos(A+B)] with A = wt and B = wt - phi gives a constant term carrying the whole average plus a double-frequency ripple. Option a keeps the ripple at w, forgetting that A + B = 2wt - phi. Option b interchanges sine and cosine, which would make the average power zero for a resistor. Option d is the correct form only for phi = 0 and then multiplies by cos(phi) again, double-counting the power factor.

questions.q: The instantaneous power in an AC circuit oscillates at:
options: the supply frequency f, in phase with the current
a frequency that depends on the power factor
questions.concept: Power ripple frequency is 2f
questions.why: v and i each change sign twice per cycle and, in a resistor, do so together, so their product completes two cycles for every one of the supply - the 2wt term in the decomposition. Option a confuses the frequency of the current with that of its square, option c inverts the relation, and option d confuses the ripple's frequency, always 2f, with its offset, which is what cos(phi) sets.

questions.q: An ideal inductor on an AC supply carries a large current and has a large voltage across it, yet its average power is zero. The reason is that:
options: an ideal inductor carries no current, so p = vi is zero at every instant
the current averages to zero over a cycle, and the average of a product is the product of the averages
X_L is measured in ohms but is an imaginary quantity, so I^2 X_L cannot be a real power
the stored magnetic energy is returned to the source in the quarter-cycle after it is taken
questions.concept: A reactance stores and returns energy rather than converting it
questions.why: Over one quarter-cycle the source pours energy into the magnetic field, up to (1/2)L*I0^2, and over the next it is returned, so p(t) is positive for two quarter-cycles and equally negative for the other two and the mean is exactly zero. Option a is false, since the current is V/X_L. Option b invokes a rule that does not exist: a resistor's current also averages to zero, yet its power does not. Option c confuses complex-number bookkeeping with physics; I^2 X_L is a real number of var.

questions.q: For a series AC circuit, the power factor is:
options: cos(phi) = R/Z, the ratio of real power to apparent power
sin(phi) = X/Z, the ratio of reactive power to apparent power
tan(phi) = X/R, the ratio of reactive power to real power
cos(phi) = Z/R, so a circuit with reactance has a power factor above 1
questions.concept: Power factor is P/S = cos(phi) = R/Z
questions.why: PF = P/S = (VI cos phi)/(VI) = cos(phi), and from the impedance triangle cos(phi) = R/Z. Option b is the reactive factor Q/S, a real quantity but not the power factor. Option c is tan(phi) = Q/P. Option d inverts the ratio and would give values above 1, which is impossible: no circuit can consume more watts than the volt-amperes it draws.

questions.q: Two loads each draw the same rms current from the same supply; one has a power factor of 0.80 lagging, the other 0.80 leading. Comparing them:
options: the lagging load consumes more, because inductive loads are the ones that do mechanical work
the leading load consumes negative real power, since energy flows back to the source
both consume the same real power, and differ only in the sign of their reactive power
the leading load has the larger apparent power, because of its extra charging current
questions.concept: cos(phi) is an even function, so the sign of phi lives entirely in Q
questions.why: P = VI cos(phi) and cos(+36.9 deg) = cos(-36.9 deg) = 0.80, so both consume the same watts; what differs is Q = VI sin(phi), positive for the lagging load and negative for the leading one, which is exactly why one can correct the other. Option a substitutes an application for the mathematics. Option b confuses a leading current with reverse power flow. Option d is wrong because S = VI depends only on the two magnitudes, which are equal by hypothesis.

questions.q: A slide states that in a purely reactive AC circuit 'the power can be calculated using P = V x I x sin(theta)'. The correct reading of that expression is:
options: it is right as written - a purely reactive circuit consumes V*I*sin(theta) watts
it is the reactive power, measured in var; the real power consumed is zero
it is the apparent power, which for a purely reactive circuit is equal to V*I
it is the real power for a capacitor only; for an inductor the sign is reversed
questions.concept: V*I*sin(theta) is reactive power Q, not power consumed
questions.why: It measures the rate at which energy is borrowed from and returned to the source. In a purely reactive circuit theta = +/-90 deg, so V*I*sin(theta) = +/-V*I: the whole apparent power is reactive and the real power is zero. Option a contradicts the deck's own correct statement that reactances do not dissipate energy. Option c confuses Q with S, which happen to be equal in magnitude here only because P = 0. Option d invents a distinction between L and C; both dissipate nothing.

questions.q: Over part of every cycle p(t) is negative. This means that:
options: the current has reversed direction, as it does twice in every AC cycle
the circuit is generating energy, which is how reactance raises the power factor
the measurement is faulty, since a wattmeter reading is always positive
energy is flowing from the circuit back to the source at that instant
questions.concept: Negative instantaneous power is a reverse flow of energy
questions.why: During those instants v and i have opposite signs, so the circuit returns stored field energy to the source rather than taking it. Option a is true but irrelevant: in a resistor the current reverses too, yet v reverses with it and p stays positive. Option b confuses returning borrowed energy with creating it. Option c treats a real feature of p(t) as an instrument fault; a wattmeter reads the average, which is what stays positive for a passive load.

questions.q: Transformers and supply cables are rated in kVA rather than kW because:
options: their winding heating and core flux are set by current and voltage, not by the load's phase angle
the transformer itself consumes reactive power, which must be added to the load's watts
the power factor of a transformer is always 1, so kVA and kW are numerically equal
kVA is the larger number and so builds a safety margin into the nameplate
questions.concept: Apparent power is what limits plant, because current and voltage set the stresses
questions.why: Copper loss goes as I^2 R and core flux is set by V, so a 100 kW load at PF 0.50 stresses a transformer exactly as hard as a 200 kW load at unity power factor - hence a VA rating. Option b invents a load; the transformer's own magnetising vars are small and are not what the rating expresses. Option c is false, since a transformer's power factor is whatever its load makes it. Option d mistakes a physical limit for padding.

questions.q: Starting from p(t) = v(t)i(t), derive P_av = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi). Say precisely which term of your expression vanishes on averaging and why it vanishes, and explain what the surviving term represents physically.
questions.concept: Average power is the constant term of p(t); the double-frequency term integrates to zero
questions.why: With v = V0 sin(wt) and i = I0 sin(wt - phi), p(t) = V0*I0*sin(wt)*sin(wt - phi), and sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A-B) - cos(A+B)] gives p(t) = (V0*I0/2)[cos(phi) - cos(2wt - phi)]. The second term is a pure sinusoid of angular frequency 2w, and the integral of a sinusoid over a whole number of periods is zero, so it contributes nothing to the mean however large its amplitude. Only the first term survives, and being constant it is its own average: P_av = (V0*I0/2)cos(phi) = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi), since Vrms*Irms = (V0/sqrt2)(I0/sqrt2) = V0*I0/2. Physically the constant term is the part of the energy flow that goes one way only - the irreversible conversion in the resistance - while the 2w term is the reversible sloshing of energy into and out of the magnetic and electric fields, transporting energy back and forth but delivering none over a full cycle. Note that p(t) oscillates about P with amplitude V0*I0/2 = S, so it dips below zero whenever cos(phi) < 1.

questions.q: Explain why neither a pure inductor nor a pure capacitor dissipates any average power, although each carries current and has voltage across it. Then explain why this is the reason X_L and X_C enter the impedance at right angles to R rather than being added to it.
questions.concept: Reactances store and return energy, so their voltage is entirely in quadrature with the current
questions.why: In an inductor the voltage leads the current by exactly 90 deg, so p = vi is positive while both have the same sign and negative while they have opposite signs; because the offset is a quarter of a period the positive and negative areas over one cycle are exactly equal. Energy taken from the source builds the magnetic field, peak store (1/2)L*I0^2, and is handed back intact in the next quarter-cycle. The same argument runs for a capacitor with the current leading by 90 deg and the store (1/2)C*V0^2. Formally cos(+/-90 deg) = 0, so P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = 0. Why this makes them perpendicular: the average power delivered to an element depends only on the component of its voltage that is in phase with the current. A resistor's voltage is entirely in phase (all of it does work); a reactance's voltage is entirely in quadrature (none of it does work). In phase and in quadrature are perpendicular directions in the phasor plane, so the resistive and reactive drops - and hence R and X - combine by Pythagoras, Z = sqrt(R^2 + X^2), not arithmetically. If they simply added, a reactance would raise the dissipation exactly as a resistance does, which the zero-average result forbids.

questions.q: Define real, reactive and apparent power, giving the unit of each, and explain why S^2 = P^2 + Q^2 rather than S = P + Q. Explain also why a power factor of 0.60 tells you the ratio of two of these quantities but not whether the current leads or lags.
questions.concept: The power triangle - three quantities, three units, combined in quadrature
questions.why: Real (true, active) power P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = I^2 R, in watts (W), is the rate of irreversible conversion to heat or work and the only one that is consumed. Reactive power Q = Vrms*Irms*sin(phi) = I^2 X, in volt-amperes reactive (var), is the rate at which energy is exchanged with the magnetic and electric fields, averaging to zero net transfer. Apparent power S = Vrms*Irms = I^2 Z, in volt-amperes (VA), is the product of the two meter readings and fixes the current the conductors must carry. S^2 = P^2 + Q^2 because P follows the component of the current in phase with the voltage and Q the component in quadrature with it; these are perpendicular components of the same current, so multiplying each by Vrms gives two perpendicular sides of a right-angled triangle with S as hypotenuse - the power triangle is the impedance triangle scaled by I^2. Adding arithmetically double-counts: 800 W with 600 var is 1000 VA, not 1400 VA. A power factor of 0.60 fixes P/S = 0.60 but not the sign of phi, because cos is an even function: phi = +53.1 deg and phi = -53.1 deg give the same cosine. Only the sign of sin(phi), i.e. of Q, distinguishes inductive (current lagging) from capacitive (current leading), which is why a power factor must always be quoted as lagging or leading.

questions.q: The lecture deck states both that 'in a purely reactive AC circuit the power can be calculated using P = V*I*sin(theta)' and, two slides later, that 'reactances do not dissipate energy'. Explain why these cannot both be true as written, identify which one is right, and say what the other expression actually measures.
questions.concept: The deck's P = V*I*sin(theta) is reactive power; its later statement is the correct one
questions.why: The two are contradictory because the first assigns a non-zero consumption to a circuit that the second says consumes nothing: in a purely reactive circuit theta = +/-90 deg, so V*I*sin(theta) = +/-V*I, the entire apparent power - the largest value the expression can take, in a circuit that by the second statement dissipates none of it. The second statement is correct. A reactance stores energy for a quarter-cycle and returns it in the next, so its average power is exactly zero; equivalently P = V*I*cos(theta) with theta = +/-90 deg gives cos(theta) = 0. The first expression is really Q = Vrms*Irms*sin(theta), the reactive power, in volt-amperes reactive (var) - the amplitude of the energy shuttling back and forth, not a rate of consumption. The correct general statement is P = Vrms*Irms*cos(theta) = Irms^2 R, which automatically returns zero for a pure reactance (R = 0) and Vrms*Irms for a pure resistance (theta = 0). A useful sanity check on any such formula: it must give zero for R = 0 and must never exceed Vrms*Irms.

checks.topic: Data types, variables and programme objects as concepts, exactly as the two decks give them: what a programme contains besides its instructions, what a data type is and the three basic types in C, the deck's rule for a variable definition and its sentence that a definition is also a declaration but not every declaration is a definition, why variable names are replaced by memory addresses, the six operator categories by name, and what a programme object is - state in variables, behaviour in methods, who may reach the state, and structure versus union versus class.

questions.q: The slides state: "A variable definition is also a declaration, but not all variable declarations are definitions." Taken at face value, what does that sentence assert?
options: A definition is a declaration that also gives the variable a starting value, so 'int x;' is a declaration and 'int x = 0;' is a definition
A declaration is what you write inside a function body; a definition is what you write outside all functions, at the top of the file
Every declaration is a definition, but not every definition is a declaration
Every definition is also a declaration, so the definitions sit inside the declarations - and there can be declarations that stop short of defining
questions.concept: The sentence asserts one implication and denies the other
questions.why: The sentence has a direction. Definition implies declaration is asserted ('a variable definition IS ALSO a declaration'); the converse is denied ('NOT ALL variable declarations are definitions'). So writing a definition always counts as declaring the name and its type, and there exist declarations that do less - the week's summary sheet glosses the shortfall as reserving the storage. Option (C) is that same sentence read backwards, which is the commonest error here. Option (A) confuses definition with initialisation: 'int x;' is a complete definition whose bytes simply hold whatever was there before. Option (B) invents a rule about where each is written; both may appear inside a function or outside one. Note what the deck does with the sentence: it poses it as a question - 'What does this mean?' - and the next slide changes the subject without answering, so the relationship is quotable but the explanation of it comes from the summary sheet.

questions.q: "Variable names are not stored inside the computer memory; the compiler replaces them with memory location addresses." Which conclusion follows from that?
options: A variable's name should be kept short, because every extra character in a name occupies extra memory while the program runs
The name exists only while the program is being compiled; at run time the machine works from an address, so a consistent rename cannot change what the compiled program does
Because the name is discarded, the value stored in a variable cannot be read back once something else has been assigned to it
The compiler must build a table of names into the finished program, so that the running program can look each of its variables up by name at the moment it needs the value
questions.concept: Names are compile-time; addresses are run-time
questions.why: Once compilation is finished every use of the name has become 'the bytes at such-and-such an address', so the identifier plays no further part - long names cost nothing at run time and a consistent rename produces the same machine code. Option (A) is the belief the deck's sentence exists to correct, and the usual excuse for cryptic one-letter names. Option (C) confuses discarding the NAME with discarding the VALUE; the bytes at the address stay where they are and may be read as often as you like. Option (D) describes a debug symbol table, which exists for the debugger, not so that a program can find its own variables - it is exactly the arrangement the quoted sentence says C does not use.

questions.q: What does specifying a data type actually accomplish, on the deck's own definition?
options: It fixes the type and the size of the data associated with the variable
It restricts what the variable may be called, since each of the types permits its own different set of names
It fixes the variable's value for the rest of the program, so that later statements cannot change it
It makes the program convert whatever the user types at the keyboard into the right form automatically
questions.concept: A data type fixes the type and the size of the data
questions.why: The deck's wording is that 'data type is used for specifying the type of a variable' and that data types 'determine the type and size of data associated with variables'. That is why the deck also tells you to 'select the data type according your programme logic and need' - the choice is about what kind of value the variable will hold and how much room it needs. Option (B) inverts the two halves of a definition; the naming rules do not change with the type. Option (C) describes a constant, not a type: a type says what kind of value may be stored, never that it may not be stored again. Option (D) confuses declaring a type with input conversion, which is a separate matter entirely.

questions.q: Which list gives the three basic types the deck names for the C language?
questions.concept: The three basic types in C
questions.why: The deck says it twice: 'There are three basic types in the C language: characters, integer, and floating-point numbers.' Option (D) names two things the deck introduces in the other lesson of the same week, and introduces as USER-DEFINED data types built out of members - which is precisely what separates them from the basic types. Option (B) adds strings, which C builds out of characters rather than providing as a basic type. Option (A) adds Booleans, which belong to a later week and which C represents as integers in any case.

questions.q: "An operator is a symbol that tells the compiler to perform specific mathematical or logical functions." The deck lists six types of operator that C provides. Which list is the deck's?
options: Arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment and misc
Arithmetic, relational, logical, iterative, assignment and misc
Arithmetic, comparison, Boolean, bitwise, storage and special
Arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, conditional and recursive
questions.concept: The six operator categories, by name
questions.why: The deck lists exactly these six after its definition of an operator: arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment and misc. Option (B) swaps bitwise for 'iterative', which is a control-flow idea belonging to a later week, not a kind of operator. Option (D) swaps assignment and misc for 'conditional' and 'recursive' - recursion is a Week 10 topic and is not an operator at all. Option (C) renames four of the six with plausible synonyms, which is the trap: the deck gives these names, and 'comparison' or 'Boolean' will not do in an answer that asks for the deck's list.

questions.q: The deck says a computer program includes more than just instructions. What else does it say a program contains?
options: Header files and the libraries that they import
Nothing else at all; a programme is only a series of instructions, and there is nothing besides them in it
Data, and the various memory addresses in which the instructions work
questions.concept: What a program contains besides its instructions
questions.why: The deck defines a programme as 'a series of instructions that causes a computer or a microcontroller to perform a particular task' and then immediately adds: 'A computer program includes more than just instructions. It also contains data and various memory addresses in which the instructions work to perform a specific task.' Those two additions are why the rest of the week exists - data is what needs types and variables, and addresses are what the variable names become. Option (C) is the definition with its second half removed. Options (A) and (B) name things that appear in the SOURCE FILE; neither is what the deck says the program contains.

questions.q: In a programme object, where does the state live, where does the behaviour live, and who may reach the state?
options: State lives in methods and behaviour in variables, and any part of the programme may reach either
State and behaviour both live in variables, and the methods only display them
The state of an object is stored in variables and its behaviour is described by methods, and only that object's own methods may reach its variables
State lives in variables and behaviour in methods, but every object of a given kind shares one single set of variables with every other object of that same kind
questions.concept: State in variables, behaviour in methods, and who may reach the variables
questions.why: The deck states all three parts. 'In programming, an object is defined by its state and behaviour. The state of an object is stored in variables and the behaviour of objects is described by methods.' 'This means that every object will have their own variables and methods.' And: 'Methods are central to how programme objects work because only the methods of a particular object have access to the variables or state of that object', with the companion sentence that 'different objects can only interact with each other through their own individual methods'. Option (A) swaps the two and then removes the restriction, which is the whole point. Option (D) gets the mapping right and then denies 'every object will have their own variables and methods'. Option (B) leaves the object with no behaviour at all.

questions.q: A 'struct Dog' and a 'union Dog' are written with the same three members - char name[20], char breed[20], char colour[20]. On the deck's definitions, what is the difference?
options: The union may group members of different types while the structure requires every member to be of the same type, which is why this union is the more useful of the two here
In the structure each member has its own storage, so all three hold values at once; in the union all members start at the same location, so only one member's value is represented at a time
The structure is a user-defined data type while the union is one of C's built-in types, which is why the union needs no struct-style keyword before it
The union is a structure that has been given methods as well as variables, which is what makes it the halfway step between a structure and a class
questions.concept: Structure vs union - same syntax, different memory layout
questions.why: The deck defines both with the same phrase about grouping items of possibly different types into a single type, so that wording cannot separate them; the difference it gives is that 'all of its members start at the same location in memory' and that 'a union variable can represent the value of only one of its members at a time'. On the summary sheet's three char[20] members that makes the struct 60 bytes with three independent strings and the union 20 bytes in which writing breed overwrites name. Option (A) is false of both - the deck says 'possibly different types' of each. Option (C) is false in both halves: both are user-defined and both need their keyword. Option (D) confuses union with class, which is the one that adds methods.

questions.q: State what a data type is in the deck's own words, name the three basic types it gives for C, and quote the deck's rule for writing a variable definition. Then explain what "determine the type and size of data associated with variables" gives the programmer, and why the deck says to select the data type "according your programme logic and need" - use the deck's own three basic types to show the choice being made.
questions.concept: A data type as a size and a kind, and the definition rule
questions.why: THE DEFINITIONS. 'Data type is used for specifying the type of a variable. They determine the type and size of data associated with variables.' 'There are three basic types in the C language: characters, integer, and floating-point numbers.' THE RULE: 'Variable definition always includes "data type" followed by "variable name"' - so 'int count;', 'float average;', 'char grade;' - and the deck adds that 'before using a variable, you should always define it by using appropriate data type'. WHAT TYPE AND SIZE GIVE YOU. Two separate things. SIZE is how much room the definition sets aside, which is why the same programme can hold a single letter cheaply and a measurement expensively. TYPE is the kind of value those bytes stand for, which is what makes one of them a letter and the other a measurement, and which is why the deck pairs the words in one sentence rather than naming one of them. Together they settle what the variable can hold and therefore what can sensibly be done with it. WHY THE CHOICE IS MADE FROM THE PROBLEM. The deck's instruction is that you 'can select the data type according your programme logic and need', which is the same lesson as its slide on representing a problem as data: you look at the quantity in the problem and ask what kind of value it is. A letter grade is one character, so 'char grade;'. A count of students is a whole number, so 'int count;'. An average or a measurement is not a whole number, so 'float average;'. The three basic types are three answers to one question - what kind of value is this? - and the definition rule is how the answer is written down: data type first, variable name second.

questions.q: The deck says: "When we programme problems, we represent the problem as data (or variable) and the variable is stored and processed by the computer." Explain what that instruction asks a programmer to do, then answer the deck's own example - to find the average of the first five multiples of 9, what are the variables? - naming each variable, giving a definition for it in the deck's required form, and saying what value it would hold. Then do the same for a second problem: print the letter grade of a student from a single score.
questions.concept: Representing a problem as data, with the deck's own example
questions.why: WHAT THE INSTRUCTION ASKS. Before any code is written, the problem is read for the QUANTITIES it involves - the things whose values the computer will have to hold and work on - and each of those becomes a variable with a name and a data type. The deck's sentence puts it as representing the problem AS DATA, and the reason it matters is in the second half: the variable 'is stored and processed by the computer', so anything the machine has to remember or change must have been given a variable first. THE DECK'S EXAMPLE - the average of the first five multiples of 9. The multiples themselves are 9, 18, 27, 36 and 45. What varies as the programme runs is: the multiple currently being handled, the running total they are added into, how many there are, and the average that comes out. So, using the deck's rule of data type followed by variable name: 'int multiple;' holds 9, then 18, then 27, then 36, then 45 in turn; 'int sum;' ends holding 135; 'int count;' holds 5; 'float average;' holds 27. (The five multiples could equally be held in five variables, but one variable reused plus a running sum is the form the arithmetic actually needs.) Notice that 9 and 5 are not by themselves the variables - they are numbers mentioned in the wording of the problem, and mistaking those for the data is the usual first error. THE SECOND PROBLEM - a letter grade from a score. The quantities are the score that comes in and the grade that goes out: 'int score;' holds, say, 72, and 'char grade;' holds a single character such as 'A'. The types follow from the deck's instruction to select a data type according to the programme logic and need: a score is a whole number, and a grade is one character, which is exactly what the basic type 'characters' is for.

questions.q: Explain how a real-world object's state and behaviour become parts of a programme object, and what the deck means by "only the methods of a particular object have access to the variables of that object" and "different objects can only interact with each other through their own individual methods". Then explain the mechanism by which that single restriction produces the four benefits the deck claims - independent creation and maintenance, reuse in various parts of the programme, safe removal and replacement, and information hiding.
questions.concept: State in variables, behaviour in methods, and encapsulation as the mechanism behind every benefit
questions.why: Real-world objects have two main characteristics, state and behaviour: the deck's dog has the state name, colour, breed, hungry and the behaviour barking, fetching, wagging its tail. In a programme object the mapping is exact - the state of an object is stored in variables and the behaviour is described by methods - and every object has its OWN variables and methods, so two dog objects have two separate name variables. The restriction is that the variables are not reachable from outside: the only doors into an object's state are the methods it publishes, which the summary sheet's access specifiers private and public control, and which data encapsulation names (hiding the implementation details so the user interacts only through public methods). Each benefit follows from that one fact. INDEPENDENT CREATION AND MAINTENANCE: since no outside code touches the variables, nothing outside can depend on how they are arranged, so the internals can be rewritten and every user still works, provided the methods keep their signatures. REUSE: the object carries its own state, so it does not depend on a surrounding context and needs no shared global set up before it will work. REMOVAL AND REPLACEMENT ('similar to how a car works'): the rest of the code only ever spoke to the object through its methods, so a replacement offering the same methods drops straight in. INFORMATION HIDING: because state is reachable only through methods, the author chooses which methods exist and therefore controls how much is shared - a get_name() with no matching setter makes the name readable and unchangeable, which no arrangement of loose variables can enforce.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a structure, a union and a class as the deck defines them, saying for each what it can hold and how its members sit in memory. Given the three members char name[20], char breed[20], char colour[20], state the size of the structure and the size of the union as the week's summary sheet gives them, and explain why they differ. Then say what a programmer gains by choosing a union, and what they must be careful about in return.
questions.concept: Structure, union and class - what each holds and how it is laid out
questions.why: A STRUCTURE is 'a user-defined data type that can be used to group items of possibly different types into a single type', defined with the struct keyword and accessed with the dot syntax; it holds variables only, and each member gets its own storage, so all members hold values at once and the size of the structure is the sum of its members. A UNION is 'defined in the same way' and also holds variables only, but 'all of its members start at the same location in memory', overlapping completely, so 'a union variable can represent the value of only one of its members at a time' and its size is the size of its LARGEST member. A CLASS is 'similar to structures but in addition to having variables, classes also usually have methods or functions' - the dog class has name, breed, colour and get_name() - and the summary sheet adds the access specifiers public and private that make encapsulation enforceable rather than conventional. SIZES: each member here is char[20], so sizeof(struct Dog) = 20 + 20 + 20 = 60 bytes because the three arrays sit at three different offsets, while sizeof(union Dog) = 20 bytes because all three start at the same location and share the same 20 bytes; a union must be big enough for its largest member and no bigger. WHAT THE UNION BUYS: memory. Where a value is known to be one of several alternatives and never more than one at a time, the union stores it in the space of the largest alternative rather than the sum of all of them, which matters in the small-memory settings C is used in. THE PRICE: nothing in the union records which alternative is live. Writing one member destroys the others, and reading a member that was not the last one written gives the previous member's bytes read as the wrong kind of value, which is meaningless rather than merely wrong. The programmer must carry that knowledge separately - conventionally by wrapping the union in a STRUCTURE together with a small tag variable recording which member is currently valid, and checking the tag before every read.

checks.topic: Problems-only session on Week 7 integration. Apply ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c to polynomials, negative powers and fractions rewritten as powers; then evaluate definite integrals by the Fundamental Theorem, F(x)|ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Includes both tasks the lecturer set — ∫(2x² − 6x − 3)dx and ∫₋₁²(7x − 5)dx — plus limits that are negative, antiderivatives that carry a minus sign, and one worked solution to diagnose.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫(x³ + 1/x³)dx.
questions.concept: Power rule across a positive and a negative exponent in one integrand
questions.why: The second term is x⁻³; the new power is −3 + 1 = −2 and you divide by −2, giving x⁻²/(−2) = −1/(2x²). Option 1 keeps the term positive, the classic slip of ignoring that the divisor is negative. Option 3 subtracts 1 from the exponent instead of adding, producing x⁻⁴. Option 4 differentiates both terms instead of integrating them.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫(3/x⁵)dx.
questions.concept: Rewriting a fraction as a negative power before applying the rule
questions.why: Rewrite as ∫3x⁻⁵dx; the new power is −4, so 3x⁻⁴/(−4) = −3/(4x⁴). Option 1 loses the sign that dividing by −4 produces. Option 2 goes the wrong way on the exponent, to −6, which is the differentiation direction. Option 3 divides the 3 away as well as using the wrong constant — it comes from mistakenly writing x⁻⁴/(−2).

questions.q: The first TASK slide asks for ∫(2x² − 6x − 3)dx. What is it?
questions.concept: Term-by-term power rule on the lecturer's own task
questions.why: 2x³/3, then 6x²/2 = 3x², then 3x. Option 2 forgets to divide the 6 by the new power 2. Option 3 forgets to divide the 2 by the new power 3. Option 4 leaves the constant term −3 unintegrated; ∫3dx = 3x, by the power rule with n = 0, not 3. Differentiating option 1 returns 2x² − 6x − 3, which none of the others do.

questions.q: A student writes: ∫₂³(1/x²)dx = (1/x)|₂³ = 1/3 − 1/2 = −1/6. What is the actual value, and what went wrong?
options: 1/6; the limits were taken in the wrong order
1/6; the antiderivative of x⁻² is −1/x, not 1/x
−1/6; the sign is right but the constant of integration was dropped
questions.concept: Getting the antiderivative of x⁻² right, sign included
questions.why: x⁻² integrates to x⁻¹/(−1) = −1/x, so the correct working is (−1/x)|₂³ = −(1/3 − 1/2) = 1/6. Option 1 accepts a wrong antiderivative — differentiating 1/x gives −1/x², not 1/x². Option 2 identifies the right answer for the wrong reason: the limits were in the correct order, upper minus lower, so reversing them would introduce a second error rather than fix this one. Option 4 is doubly wrong: the sign is not right, and a definite integral has no constant.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁴ 6x dx.
questions.concept: Fundamental Theorem applied as in the lecturer's Example 1
questions.why: F(x) = 3x², so 3x²|₀⁴ = 3(4² − 0²) = 3(16) = 48. Option 1 substitutes into the integrand 6x rather than into F. Option 2 uses 6x² as the antiderivative, forgetting to divide by the new power. Option 3 uses x² and drops the coefficient entirely.

questions.q: The second TASK slide asks for ∫₋₁²(7x − 5)dx. What is it?
questions.concept: Definite integral with a negative lower limit and a negative result
questions.why: F(x) = 7x²/2 − 5x. At x = 2: 14 − 10 = 4. At x = −1: 7/2 + 5 = 17/2, because −5(−1) = +5. So 4 − 17/2 = −9/2. Option 2 computes lower minus upper. Option 3 comes from writing −5(−1) as −5, giving 4 − 3/2. Option 4 evaluates the upper limit and forgets to subtract the lower one. A negative answer is legitimate here and should not prompt a hunt for a lost minus sign.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋₁⁴(3x² − 6)dx.
questions.concept: Two-term definite integral, cubing a negative limit
questions.why: F(x) = x³ − 6x, so (4³ − 24) − ((−1)³ − 6(−1)) = (64 − 24) − (−1 + 6) = 40 − 5 = 35. Option 1 arises from taking (−1)³ = +1. Option 2 drops the −6x term altogether, leaving 64 + 1. Option 4 mishandles the sign of −6(−1) at the lower limit, using −6 − 1 instead of −1 + 6.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋₂¹ 3x² dx.
questions.concept: Subtracting a negative value of the antiderivative
questions.why: F(x) = x³, so x³|₋₂¹ = 1³ − (−2)³ = 1 − (−8) = 9. Option 1 subtracts 8 instead of −8, i.e. treats (−2)³ as +8. Option 3 gets the magnitude of that slip but not its sign. Option 4 reverses the limits. The whole question turns on one fact — an odd power keeps the sign of a negative base — and no amount of vocabulary substitutes for it.

questions.q: Work the first TASK slide in full: evaluate ∫(2x² − 6x − 3)dx, then verify your answer.
questions.concept: Full solution plus verification by differentiation
questions.why: A good answer splits the integral term by term, applies ∫xⁿdx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c to each — 2x³/3, 6x²/2 = 3x², 3x from the constant with n = 0 — assembles (2/3)x³ − 3x² − 3x + c, keeps the constant of integration, and then differentiates the result to recover 2x² − 6x − 3. Credit the verification step explicitly: it is the deck's own justification for the whole method, and it is the only check available since the slide gives no answer.

questions.q: Work the second TASK slide in full: evaluate ∫₋₁²(7x − 5)dx. Show the substitution at x = −1 explicitly, term by term.
questions.concept: Definite integral with a negative limit, written out
questions.why: A good answer states F(x) = 7x²/2 − 5x, then substitutes: at x = 2, 7(2)²/2 − 5(2) = 14 − 10 = 4; at x = −1, 7(−1)²/2 − 5(−1) = 7/2 + 5 = 17/2, spelling out that (−1)² = 1 and that subtracting a negative gives +5. It concludes 4 − 17/2 = −9/2 in the order F(b) − F(a), and should note that no + c appears and that a negative value is a legitimate answer rather than a sign error.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₂³(1/x²)dx following the lecturer's Example 3: state f(x) as a power, state F(x), and factor the minus sign out of the evaluation.
questions.concept: Reproducing the deck's definite-integral example with negative powers
questions.why: A good answer writes f(x) = 1/x² = x⁻², obtains F(x) = x⁻¹/(−1) = −1/x, and then evaluates as the slide does: (−1/x)|₂³ = −(1/3 − 1/2). It should carry out the bracket first, 1/3 − 1/2 = −1/6, and then negate to get +1/6, noting that the order inside the bracket is still upper minus lower — the minus that was factored out sits in front of the whole bracket and does not swap the limits.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫(2/x⁷)dx. State the value of n you are using and show the division step.
questions.concept: Example 3 reproduced, with the exponent identified
questions.why: A good answer rewrites 2/x⁷ as 2x⁻⁷ and says explicitly that n = −7, computes the new exponent −7 + 1 = −6, divides by it — 2·x⁻⁶/(−6) — and simplifies 2/(−6) to −1/3, giving −1/(3x⁶) + c with the constant retained. It should identify the division by −6 as the source of the minus sign, and can verify by differentiating −(1/3)x⁻⁶ to get 2x⁻⁷.

checks.topic: Numerical work on power in an A.C. circuit: substituting into X_L = 2*pi*f*L and X_C = 1/(2*pi*f*C), computing Z, I and cos(phi), then P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) = Irms^2 R with Q and S, checking by S^2 = P^2 + Q^2, and doing power-factor correction, resonance and instantaneous-power calculations

questions.q: A coil of resistance 9.0 ohm and inductance 38.2 mH is connected across a 120 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The rms current drawn is:
questions.concept: Reactance first, then combine with R in quadrature
questions.why: X_L = 2*pi*f*L = 2*pi*(50)(0.0382) = 12.0 ohm; Z = sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(225) = 15.0 ohm; I = 120/15.0 = 8.00 A. Option a is 120/9, ignoring the reactance. Option c is 120/(9 + 12), adding R and X arithmetically instead of in quadrature. Option d is 120/12, ignoring the resistance.

questions.q: For that same coil on the 120 V rms supply, the real power consumed is:
questions.concept: P = I^2 R; only the resistance dissipates
questions.why: P = (8.00)^2 (9.0) = 576 W, confirmed by P = V*I*cos(phi) = (120)(8.00)(0.600) = 576 W. Option a is S = V*I = 960 VA with the power factor left out. Option b is V^2/R = 14400/9, using the whole supply voltage across R although only V_R = I*R = 72 V is there. Option c is I^2 X_L = 768 var, the reactive power, which nothing consumes.

questions.q: For that same coil on the 120 V rms supply, the power factor is:
questions.concept: PF = cos(phi) = R/Z, and an inductive circuit lags
questions.why: 9/15 = 0.600, and since the reactance is inductive the current lags the voltage, so it is 0.600 lagging. Option b is sin(phi) = X/Z = 12/15, the reactive factor. Option c has the right number but the wrong sense, which would require a net capacitive reactance. Option d is Z/R = 15/9, an inverted ratio that is impossible: a power factor above 1 would mean more watts consumed than volt-amperes drawn.

questions.q: A series circuit has R = 16 ohm, X_L = 30 ohm and X_C = 18 ohm across a 100 V rms supply. The impedance is:
questions.concept: Net reactance first: X_L and X_C subtract, then combine with R in quadrature
questions.why: X = 30 - 18 = 12 ohm, so Z = sqrt(16^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(400) = 20 ohm. Option a adds all three as though they were series resistances. Option b is sqrt(16^2 + 48^2) = 50.6 ohm, adding the two reactances instead of subtracting them. Option d is the net reactance alone, ignoring R.

questions.q: For that same series circuit (R = 16 ohm, X_L = 30 ohm, X_C = 18 ohm, 100 V rms), the real power consumed is:
questions.concept: P = I^2 R after finding I from the full impedance
questions.why: I = 100/20 = 5.00 A, so P = (25.0)(16) = 400 W, confirmed by V*I*cos(phi) = (100)(5.00)(0.800) = 400 W. Option b is S = V*I = 500 VA with the power factor omitted. Option c is I^2 X = (25.0)(12) = 300 var, the reactive power. Option d is V^2/R = 10000/16, using the supply voltage across R rather than V_R = 80 V, and 80^2/16 = 400 W.

questions.q: For that same series circuit (R = 16 ohm, X_L = 30 ohm, X_C = 18 ohm), the circuit is:
options: capacitive, with the current leading the supply voltage by 36.9 deg
inductive, with the current lagging the supply voltage by 36.9 deg
inductive, with the current lagging the supply voltage by 53.1 deg
at resonance, since R is greater than the net reactance
questions.concept: X_L > X_C makes the circuit inductive; tan(phi) = X/R fixes the angle
questions.why: The net reactance is +12 ohm, so the current lags, and tan(phi) = 12/16 = 0.750 gives phi = 36.9 deg, consistent with cos(phi) = 0.800. Option a has the character backwards, which would need X_C > X_L. Option c has the character right but inverts the tangent, using R/X = 16/12 to get 53.1 deg. Option d confuses resistance dominating the net reactance with resonance, which requires X_L = X_C exactly.

questions.q: R = 20 ohm, L = 0.50 H and C = 8.0 microfarad are in series across a 60 V rms supply driven at the resonant frequency. The current is:
questions.concept: At series resonance the reactances cancel and Z falls to R
questions.why: w0 = 1/sqrt(LC) = 1/sqrt(0.50 x 8.0e-6) = 1/sqrt(4.0e-6) = 500 rad/s, so X_L = X_C = 250 ohm and Z = R = 20 ohm, giving I = 60/20 = 3.00 A, a maximum. Option a is the parallel (rejector) resonance result, where the impedance is a maximum, applied to a series circuit. Option b is 60/sqrt(20^2 + 500^2), adding the reactances instead of subtracting them. Option c is 60/250, using X_L alone as the impedance.

questions.q: In that same resonant circuit (R = 20 ohm, L = 0.50 H, C = 8.0 microfarad, 60 V rms), the rms voltage across the inductor is:
questions.concept: At resonance V_L and V_C are equal and opposite, and each can greatly exceed the supply
questions.why: V_L = I*X_L = (3.00)(250) = 750 V, and V_C is the same 750 V in antiphase, so they cancel in the vector sum and the supply still sees only V_R = (3.00)(20) = 60 V. The factor 750/60 = 12.5 is the Q-factor X_L/R = 250/20. Option a assumes no drop can exceed the supply. Option b confuses V_L and V_C cancelling each other with each being zero. Option d quotes the reactance in ohms as though it were a voltage.

questions.q: A coil of resistance 40 ohm and inductance 95.5 mH is connected across a 240 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Find X_L, Z, the rms current, the power factor, and P, Q and S. Verify P and Q by a second route and check the power triangle.
questions.concept: The full power set for a series RL circuit, cross-checked two ways
questions.why: X_L = 2*pi*f*L = 2*pi*(50)(0.0955) = 30.0 ohm. Z = sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = sqrt(2500) = 50.0 ohm. I = 240/50.0 = 4.80 A. cos(phi) = R/Z = 40/50 = 0.800 lagging, phi = 36.9 deg with the current lagging since the reactance is inductive. P = V*I*cos(phi) = (240)(4.80)(0.800) = 921.6 W, and by the second route P = I^2 R = (23.04)(40) = 921.6 W. Q = V*I*sin(phi) = (240)(4.80)(0.600) = 691.2 var inductive, and Q = I^2 X_L = (23.04)(30) = 691.2 var. S = V*I = 1152 VA, and also I^2 Z = (23.04)(50) = 1152 VA. Triangle check: 921.6^2 + 691.2^2 = 849346.6 + 477757.4 = 1327104 = 1152^2. Note that V^2/R = 57600/40 = 1440 W is not the answer, because only V_R = I*R = 192 V sits across the resistance, and 192^2/40 = 921.6 W.

questions.q: A workshop draws 9.6 kW from a 240 V rms, 50 Hz supply at a power factor of 0.60 lagging. Find the apparent power, the line current and the reactive power; then find the parallel capacitance that would raise the power factor to unity, the new line current, and the fractional change in the I^2 R loss in the feeder cable.
questions.concept: Power-factor correction changes Q and the current, never P
questions.why: S = P/PF = 9600/0.600 = 16000 VA = 16.0 kVA. I = S/V = 16000/240 = 66.7 A. sin(phi) = 0.800, so Q = S*sin(phi) = 12800 var = 12.8 kvar lagging. To reach unity the capacitor must supply all of it, Q_C = 12800 var, so C = Q_C/(w*V^2) = 12800/[(314.16)(240^2)] = 12800/18096000 = 7.07e-4 F, about 707 microfarad. Check: I_C = w*C*V = (314.16)(7.07e-4)(240) = 53.3 A and (240)(53.3) = 12800 var, this current circulating only between the capacitor and the load, not in the feeder. With PF = 1 the supply carries only the in-phase component, I = P/V = 9600/240 = 40.0 A, down from 66.7 A. The feeder loss goes as I^2, so it falls to (40.0/66.7)^2 = 0.360, a 64 per cent reduction, while the workshop still consumes exactly 9.6 kW; the transformer requirement drops from 16.0 kVA to 9.6 kVA.

questions.q: A 110 V rms, 50 Hz supply is connected first across a 22 ohm resistor and then across a pure inductor of reactance 22 ohm. For each, write p(t), and give its peak value, its average value and its ripple frequency. Explain why the two averages differ although the two rms currents are the same.
questions.concept: The same rms current can carry all the power or none of it, depending on phi
questions.why: Resistor: I = 110/22 = 5.00 A rms; V0 = sqrt2 (110) = 155.6 V and I0 = sqrt2 (5.00) = 7.071 A, so V0*I0 = 1100 W. With v and i in phase, p = V0*I0*sin^2(wt) = 1100 sin^2(314.2 t) = 550[1 - cos(628.3 t)] W: peak 1100 W, minimum 0, average 550 W (= Vrms*Irms = 550 = I^2 R = (25.0)(22)), ripple frequency 2f = 100 Hz, and p is never negative. Inductor: X_L = 22 ohm gives the same I = 5.00 A rms, but the current lags by 90 deg, so i = -I0 cos(wt) and p = -V0*I0*sin(wt)cos(wt) = -(V0*I0/2) sin(2wt) = -550 sin(628.3 t) W: peak +/-550 W, average 0, ripple frequency again 100 Hz, and p is negative for exactly half of every cycle. The averages differ because P = Vrms*Irms*cos(phi) and the circuits differ only in phi: 0 deg for the resistor (cos phi = 1) and 90 deg for the inductor (cos phi = 0). In the resistor v and i reverse together, so the product is positive throughout and every joule delivered becomes heat; in the inductor they are a quarter-cycle apart, so the positive and negative areas are exactly equal and the energy taken to build the field, (1/2)L*I0^2 = 1.75 J per quarter-cycle, is handed straight back.

questions.q: A student analysing a series circuit with R = 8.0 ohm and X_L = 6.0 ohm on a 100 V rms supply writes: 'Z = 8 + 6 = 14 ohm, so I = 100/14 = 7.14 A and P = (100)(7.14) = 714 W.' Identify both errors, give the correct values of Z, I, PF, P, Q and S, and state the single check that would have exposed the mistake without redoing the whole calculation.
questions.concept: Reactance adds in quadrature, and V*I is apparent power, not real power
questions.why: Error 1: Z was found by adding R and X_L arithmetically. They are 90 deg apart, so Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) = sqrt(64 + 36) = 10.0 ohm, not 14 ohm. Error 2: the power factor was omitted, so (100)(7.14) is an apparent power in VA, whereas real power needs the factor cos(phi). Correct values: Z = 10.0 ohm, I = 100/10.0 = 10.0 A, cos(phi) = R/Z = 8/10 = 0.800 lagging (phi = 36.9 deg), P = (100)(10.0)(0.800) = 800 W, Q = (100)(10.0)(0.600) = 600 var, S = 1000 VA, and 800^2 + 600^2 = 1000000 = 1000^2. The check that exposes it: the real power must also equal I^2 R, and the student's own numbers give (7.14)^2 (8.0) = 408 W, nowhere near the 714 W claimed - two routes to the same quantity disagreeing by three-quarters. Equivalently, P can never exceed V*I*cos(phi) <= V*I, so claiming P = V*I asserts a power factor of 1 in a circuit that plainly has 6 ohm of reactance.
